questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: A wire with a resistance of $25 \Omega$ carries an electric current of $2.0 \text{ A}$. Determine the amount of heat developed in $1$ minute.
questions.solution:
Given:

Resistance of the wire, $R = 25 \Omega$

Current, $I = 2.0 \text{ A}$

Time, $t = 1 \text{ minute} = 60 \text{ s}$

The amount of heat developed is given by Joule's law of heating:

$H = I^2 R t$

Substituting the given values:

$H = (2.0)^2 \times 25 \times 60$

$H = 4 \times 25 \times 60$

$H = 100 \times 60$

$H = 6000 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: A heater coil has a specification of $250 \text{ V}$, $500 \text{ W}$. Determine the resistance of the coil. Additionally, what will be the resistance of a $1000 \text{ W}$ coil designed to operate at the same voltage?
questions.solution:
The power of a heater coil is given by the relation $P = \dfrac{V^2}{R}$.

Rearranging for resistance, $R = \dfrac{V^2}{P}$.

For the first coil with $V = 250 \text{ V}$ and $P = 500 \text{ W}$:

$R_1 = \dfrac{250^2}{500} = \dfrac{250 \times 250}{500} = \dfrac{250}{2} = 125 \Omega$

For the second coil with $V = 250 \text{ V}$ and $P = 1000 \text{ W}$:

$R_2 = \dfrac{250^2}{1000} = \dfrac{250 \times 250}{1000} = \dfrac{62500}{1000} = 62.5 \Omega$

The resistances are $125 \Omega$ and $62.5 \Omega$ respectively.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: A nichrome wire ($\rho = 1.0 \times 10^{-6} \Omega \text{m}$) is used to build a heater coil intended to operate at $500 \text{ W}$ when connected to a $250 \text{ V}$ supply. Determine the resistance of the coil.
questions.solution:
Given power of the heater coil, $P = 500 \text{ W}$

Operating voltage, $V = 250 \text{ V}$

The resistance of the coil is related to power and voltage by the formula:

$P = \dfrac{V^2}{R}$

Rearranging for resistance $R$:

$R = \dfrac{V^2}{P}$

Substituting the given values:

$R = \dfrac{250 \times 250}{500}$

$R = \dfrac{250}{2} = 125 \Omega$

The resistivity of nichrome is extra information and is not required to find the resistance.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: A heater coil, designed to operate at $500 \text{ W}$ across a $250 \text{ V}$ supply, is fabricated from a nichrome wire having a resistivity of $1.0 \times 10^{-6} \Omega \text{m}$. If the wire has a cross-sectional area of $0.5 \text{ mm}^2$, what is the required length of the wire?
questions.solution:
The resistance of the heater coil is given by the formula:

$R = \dfrac{V^2}{P}$

Substituting the given values $V = 250 \text{ V}$ and $P = 500 \text{ W}$:

$R = \dfrac{(250)^2}{500} = \dfrac{62500}{500} = 125 \Omega$

The resistance of a wire is related to its length $L$, cross-sectional area $A$, and resistivity $\rho$ by:

$R = \rho \dfrac{L}{A}$

Rearranging for length $L$:

$L = \dfrac{R \cdot A}{\rho}$

Given $\rho = 1.0 \times 10^{-6} \Omega \text{m}$ and $A = 0.5 \text{ mm}^2 = 0.5 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2$, substituting these values gives:

$L = \dfrac{125 \times 0.5 \times 10^{-6}}{1.0 \times 10^{-6}}$

$L = 125 \times 0.5 = 62.5 \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: A nichrome wire ($\rho = 1.0 \times 10^{-6} \Omega \text{m}$) with a cross-sectional area of $0.5 \text{ mm}^2$ is used to wrap a heater coil that operates at $500 \text{ W}$ when connected to a $250 \text{ V}$ supply. If each turn of the coil has a radius of $4.0 \text{ mm}$, approximately how many turns will the coil contain?
questions.solution:
Power of the heater coil is given by $P = \dfrac{V^2}{R}$

Resistance of the coil, $R = \dfrac{V^2}{P} = \dfrac{(250)^2}{500} = 125 \Omega$

Using the formula for resistance, $R = \rho \dfrac{L}{A}$

Total length of the wire, $L = \dfrac{RA}{\rho} = \dfrac{125 \times 0.5 \times 10^{-6}}{1.0 \times 10^{-6}} = 62.5 \text{ m}$

Length of one turn of the coil is the circumference, $C = 2\pi r = 2 \times \pi \times 4.0 \times 10^{-3} = 8\pi \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$

Number of turns, $N = \dfrac{L}{C} = \dfrac{62.5}{8\pi \times 10^{-3}}$

$N = \dfrac{62500}{8\pi} \approx \dfrac{7812.5}{3.1416} \approx 2487$

Therefore, the number of turns is approximately $2500$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: A coil with a resistance of $100 \Omega$ is connected across a battery having an emf of $6.0 \text{ V}$. Assuming all the heat developed in the coil goes into raising its temperature, and given that the heat capacity of the coil is $4.0 \text{ J K}^{-1}$, determine the time required to increase the temperature of the coil by $15^\circ \text{C}$.
questions.solution:
The power generated by the coil is given by $P = \dfrac{V^2}{R}$.

Substituting $V = 6.0 \text{ V}$ and $R = 100 \Omega$, we get:

$P = \dfrac{(6.0)^2}{100} = 0.36 \text{ J s}^{-1}$

The heat required to raise the temperature of the coil is $Q = C \Delta T$.

Substituting $C = 4.0 \text{ J K}^{-1}$ and $\Delta T = 15^\circ \text{C} = 15 \text{ K}$, we get:

$Q = 4.0 \times 15 = 60 \text{ J}$

The time required to generate this heat is $t = \dfrac{Q}{P}$.

$t = \dfrac{60}{0.36} = \dfrac{1000}{6} \text{ s}$

Converting the time into minutes:

$t = \dfrac{1000}{6 \times 60} = \dfrac{100}{36} = 2.77 \text{ minutes}$

Rounding off to one decimal place, the time required is $2.8 \text{ minutes}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: When connected across a $220 \text{ V}$ power supply, an electric bulb consumes $60 \text{ W}$ of power. What will be the power consumed if the supply voltage drops to $180 \text{ V}$, and what will it be if the supply is abruptly raised to $240 \text{ V}$?
questions.solution:
The resistance of the electric bulb is given by $R = \dfrac{V^2}{P}$

Substituting the given values, $R = \dfrac{(220)^2}{60} \, \Omega$

Assuming the resistance of the bulb remains constant, the power consumed at a new voltage $V'$ is $P' = \dfrac{(V')^2}{R}$

When the supply voltage drops to $180 \text{ V}$:

$P_1 = \dfrac{(180)^2}{\dfrac{(220)^2}{60}} = \left(\dfrac{180}{220}\right)^2 \times 60 = \dfrac{81}{121} \times 60 \approx 40.16 \text{ W}$

When the supply voltage is raised to $240 \text{ V}$:

$P_2 = \dfrac{(240)^2}{\dfrac{(220)^2}{60}} = \left(\dfrac{240}{220}\right)^2 \times 60 = \dfrac{144}{121} \times 60 \approx 71.40 \text{ W}$

The power consumed will be approximately $40 \text{ W}$ and $71 \text{ W}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: A bulb with a rating of $250 \text{ V}$, $100 \text{ W}$ is connected to a $220 \text{ V}$ power supply situated $10 \text{ m}$ away, utilizing a copper wire with a cross-sectional area of $5 \text{ mm}^2$. Determine the power consumed by the connecting wires. The resistivity of copper is $1.7 \times 10^{-8} \Omega \text{m}$.
questions.solution:
The resistance of the bulb is given by:

$R = \dfrac{V^2}{P} = \dfrac{250^2}{100} = 625 \Omega$

Since the power supply is situated $10 \text{ m}$ away, a complete circuit requires both a forward and a return path. Thus, the total length of the connecting wire is:

$l = 2 \times 10 = 20 \text{ m}$

The resistance of the connecting wire is:

$R_w = \rho \dfrac{l}{A} = \dfrac{1.7 \times 10^{-8} \times 20}{5 \times 10^{-6}} = 0.068 \Omega$

The total resistance of the circuit is:

$R_{\text{eq}} = R + R_w = 625 + 0.068 \approx 625 \Omega$

The current flowing through the circuit is:

$I = \dfrac{V'}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \dfrac{220}{625} = 0.352 \text{ A}$

The power consumed by the connecting wires is:

$P_w = I^2 R_w = (0.352)^2 \times 0.068 \approx 0.1239 \times 0.068 \approx 0.0084 \text{ W}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: An electric bulb marked $220 \text{ V}$, $100 \text{ W}$ will get fused if it is made to consume $150 \text{ W}$ or more. What maximum voltage can the bulb withstand?
questions.solution:
The resistance of the bulb is given by $R = \dfrac{V^2}{P}$.

Substituting the rated values, $R = \dfrac{220^2}{100} = 484 \Omega$.

The maximum power the bulb can withstand before fusing is $P_{max} = 150 \text{ W}$.

The maximum voltage $V_{max}$ is given by $P_{max} = \dfrac{V_{max}^2}{R}$.

$V_{max} = \sqrt{P_{max} R} = \sqrt{150 \times 484} = \sqrt{72600} \approx 269.4 \text{ V}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: An immersion heater rated at $1000 \text{ W}$, $220 \text{ V}$ is utilized to heat $0.01 \text{ m}^3$ of water. Assuming that the power is supplied at $220 \text{ V}$ and $60\%$ of the supplied power goes into heating the water, determine how long it will take to raise the temperature of the water from $15^\circ \text{C}$ to $40^\circ \text{C}$.
questions.solution:
Mass of water $m = V \times \rho = 0.01 \times 1000 = 10 \text{ kg}$

Heat required to raise the temperature of water is given by $Q = ms\Delta T$

Using the specific heat capacity of water $s = 4200 \text{ J kg}^{-1} ^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$:

$Q = 10 \times 4200 \times (40 - 15) = 1050000 \text{ J}$

Effective power utilized for heating $P_{eff} = 60\% \text{ of } 1000 \text{ W} = 600 \text{ W}$

Time taken $t = \dfrac{Q}{P_{eff}} = \dfrac{1050000}{600} = 1750 \text{ s}$

Converting to minutes, $t = \dfrac{1750}{60} \approx 29.16 \text{ minutes} \approx 29 \text{ minutes}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: A servo voltage stabiliser limits its output voltage to $220 \text{ V} \pm 1\%$. When an electric bulb rated at $220 \text{ V}$, $100 \text{ W}$ is connected to this stabiliser, determine the minimum and maximum power consumed by the bulb.
questions.solution:
The power consumed by the bulb is given by $P = \dfrac{V^2}{R}$.

For small variations, the fractional change in power is:

$\dfrac{\Delta P}{P} = 2 \dfrac{\Delta V}{V}$

Given that the voltage variation is $\pm 1\%$, we have:

$\dfrac{\Delta P}{P} = \pm 2(1\%) = \pm 2\%$

The nominal power of the bulb is $P = 100 \text{ W}$.

The variation in power is $\Delta P = \pm 2\%$ of $100 \text{ W} = \pm 2 \text{ W}$.

Therefore, the minimum power consumed is $100 - 2 = 98 \text{ W}$ and the maximum power consumed is $100 + 2 = 102 \text{ W}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: When the room temperature is $25^\circ C$, an electric kettle used for preparing tea takes $2$ minutes to boil $4$ cups of water (where $1$ cup contains $200 \text{ cc}$ of water). Calculate the cost of boiling $4$ cups of water, given that the cost of power consumption is Re $1.00$ per unit ($1$ unit $= 1000$ watt-hour).
questions.solution:
Mass of water, $m = 4 \times 200 \text{ cc} \times 1 \text{ g/cc} = 800 \text{ g} = 0.8 \text{ kg}$

Specific heat capacity of water, $s = 4200 \text{ J kg}^{-1} ^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$

Change in temperature, $\Delta T = 100^\circ\text{C} - 25^\circ\text{C} = 75^\circ\text{C}$

Heat required to boil the water, $Q = m s \Delta T$

$Q = 0.8 \times 4200 \times 75 = 252000 \text{ J}$

Since $1 \text{ unit} = 1 \text{ kWh} = 3.6 \times 10^6 \text{ J}$, the electrical energy consumed in units is:

Number of units = $\dfrac{252000}{3.6 \times 10^6} = 0.07 \text{ units}$

Given the cost of power is Re $1.00$ ($100 \text{ paise}$) per unit, the total cost is:

Cost = $0.07 \times 100 \text{ paise} = 7 \text{ paise}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: When the room temperature is $25^\circ C$, an electric kettle used for preparing tea takes $2$ minutes to boil $4$ cups of water (where $1$ cup contains $200 \text{ cc}$ of water). Given that the cost of power consumption is Re $1.00$ per unit ($1$ unit $= 1000$ watt-hour), determine the cost of boiling $4$ cups of water if the room temperature drops to $5^\circ C$.
questions.solution:
Total volume of water $= 4 \times 200 \text{ cc} = 800 \text{ cc}$.

Mass of water, $m = 800 \text{ g} = 0.8 \text{ kg}$.

Specific heat capacity of water, $s = 4200 \text{ J kg}^{-1} ^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$.

At an initial room temperature of $25^\circ \text{C}$, the heat required to boil the water ($100^\circ \text{C}$) is:

$Q_1 = ms\Delta T_1 = 0.8 \times 4200 \times (100 - 25) = 252000 \text{ J}$

The kettle takes $2 \text{ minutes}$ ($120 \text{ s}$) to boil this water. The power of the kettle is:

$P = \dfrac{Q_1}{t_1} = \dfrac{252000}{120} = 2100 \text{ W} = 2.1 \text{ kW}$

When the room temperature drops to $5^\circ \text{C}$, the new heat required to boil the water is:

$Q_2 = ms\Delta T_2 = 0.8 \times 4200 \times (100 - 5) = 319200 \text{ J}$

The time taken to boil the water at $5^\circ \text{C}$ is:

$t_2 = \dfrac{Q_2}{P} = \dfrac{319200}{2100} = 152 \text{ s}$

The electrical energy consumed in this process (in $\text{kWh}$ or units) is:

$E = P \times t_2 = 2.1 \text{ kW} \times \dfrac{152}{3600} \text{ h} = \dfrac{319.2}{3600} \text{ kWh} \approx 0.08867 \text{ units}$

Given the cost of power is $\text{Re } 1.00$ ($100 \text{ paise}$) per unit, the total cost is:

$\text{Cost} = 0.08867 \times 100 \text{ paise} = 8.867 \text{ paise}$

Rounding to the nearest integer, the cost is $9 \text{ paise}$.

Answer: $9 \text{ paise}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: The coil of an electric bulb requires $40\text{ W}$ to begin glowing. When more than $40\text{ W}$ is supplied, $60\%$ of the surplus power is converted into light, while the remainder turns into heat. The bulb consumes $100\text{ W}$ when operated at $220\text{ V}$. Determine the percentage drop in light intensity at a point if the supply voltage is reduced from $220\text{ V}$ to $200\text{ V}$.
questions.solution:
The power consumed by the bulb is given by $P = \dfrac{V^2}{R}$.

At $V_1 = 220\text{ V}$, the power consumed is $P_1 = 100\text{ W}$.
The light power output at $220\text{ V}$ is:
$L_1 = 0.6 \times (P_1 - 40) = 0.6 \times (100 - 40) = 36\text{ W}$

At $V_2 = 200\text{ V}$, assuming the resistance $R$ remains constant, the power consumed is:
$P_2 = P_1 \times \left(\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}\right)^2 = 100 \times \left(\dfrac{200}{220}\right)^2 = 100 \times \dfrac{100}{121} = \dfrac{10000}{121}\text{ W}$

The light power output at $200\text{ V}$ is:
$L_2 = 0.6 \times \left(P_2 - 40\right) = 0.6 \times \left(\dfrac{10000}{121} - 40\right) = 0.6 \times \left(\dfrac{10000 - 4840}{121}\right) = 0.6 \times \dfrac{5160}{121} = \dfrac{3096}{121}\text{ W}$

The light intensity is directly proportional to the light power output. The percentage drop in light intensity is:
$\text{Percentage drop} = \dfrac{L_1 - L_2}{L_1} \times 100\%$

$\text{Percentage drop} = \dfrac{36 - \dfrac{3096}{121}}{36} \times 100\% = \left(1 - \dfrac{3096}{36 \times 121}\right) \times 100\%$

$\text{Percentage drop} = \left(1 - \dfrac{86}{121}\right) \times 100\% = \dfrac{35}{121} \times 100\% \approx 28.92\%$

Rounding to the nearest integer, the percentage drop is $29\%$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: As illustrated in the figure, the $2.0\Omega$ resistor is immersed in a calorimeter containing water. The combined heat capacity of the calorimeter and the water is $2000\text{ J K}^{-1}$. If the circuit remains active for $15$ minutes, find the rise in the temperature of the water.
questions.solution:
The equivalent resistance of the parallel combination of the $6\Omega$ and $2\Omega$ resistors is:

$R_p = \dfrac{6 \times 2}{6 + 2} = 1.5\Omega$

The total resistance of the circuit is:

$R_{eq} = 1 + R_p = 1 + 1.5 = 2.5\Omega$

The total current drawn from the battery is:

$I = \dfrac{V}{R_{eq}} = \dfrac{6}{2.5} = 2.4\text{ A}$

The voltage across the parallel combination is:

$V_p = I \times R_p = 2.4 \times 1.5 = 3.6\text{ V}$

The power dissipated by the $2\Omega$ resistor is:

$P = \dfrac{V_p^2}{R} = \dfrac{(3.6)^2}{2} = 6.48\text{ W}$

The heat produced in the $2\Omega$ resistor in $15$ minutes ($900$ seconds) is:

$H = P \times t = 6.48 \times 900 = 5832\text{ J}$

Using the heat capacity $C = 2000\text{ J K}^{-1}$, the rise in temperature $\Delta T$ is:

$\Delta T = \dfrac{H}{C} = \dfrac{5832}{2000} = 2.916^\circ\text{C}$

Rounding to one decimal place, we get $2.9^\circ\text{C}$.
questions.question: As illustrated in the figure, the $2.0\Omega$ resistor is immersed in a calorimeter containing water. The combined heat capacity of the calorimeter and the water is $2000\text{ J K}^{-1}$. If the circuit remains active for $15$ minutes, find the rise in the temperature of the water.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: A $6\text{ V}$ ideal battery, a $1\Omega$ resistor, and a $2.0\Omega$ resistor are connected in series. The $2.0\Omega$ resistor is dipped into a calorimeter containing water. The heat capacity of the calorimeter together with the water is $2000\text{ J K}^{-1}$. Determine the rise in the temperature of the water if the circuit is active for $15$ minutes.
questions.solution:
Based on the problem description, the $6\text{ V}$ battery, the $1\Omega$ resistor, and the $2.0\Omega$ resistor are connected in series.

The equivalent resistance of the circuit is:
$R_{eq} = 1\Omega + 2.0\Omega = 3\Omega$

The current flowing through the circuit is:
$I = \dfrac{V}{R_{eq}} = \dfrac{6}{3} = 2\text{ A}$

The power dissipated by the $2.0\Omega$ resistor (which is inside the calorimeter) is:
$P = I^2 R = (2)^2 \times 2.0 = 8\text{ W}$

The heat generated in the $2.0\Omega$ resistor over a time $t = 15\text{ minutes} = 15 \times 60\text{ s} = 900\text{ s}$ is:
$H = P \times t = 8 \times 900 = 7200\text{ J}$

The rise in temperature $\Delta T$ of the calorimeter and water is given by:
$H = C \Delta T$
where $C = 2000\text{ J K}^{-1}$ is the heat capacity.

$\Delta T = \dfrac{H}{C} = \dfrac{7200}{2000} = 3.6\text{ K}$

A temperature rise of $3.6\text{ K}$ is equivalent to a rise of $3.6^\circ\text{C}$.

Answer: $3.6^\circ\text{C}$
questions.question: A $6\text{ V}$ ideal battery, a $1\Omega$ resistor, and a $2.0\Omega$ resistor are connected in series. The $2.0\Omega$ resistor is dipped into a calorimeter containing water. The heat capacity of the calorimeter together with the water is $2000\text{ J K}^{-1}$. Determine the rise in the temperature of the water if the circuit is active for $15$ minutes.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: The junction temperatures of a bismuth–silver thermocouple are kept at $0^\circ C$ and $0.001^\circ C$. Determine the developed thermo-emf (Seebeck emf). Given for bismuth–silver, $a = -46 \times 10^{-6} \text{ V }^\circ C^{-1}$ and $b = -0.48 \times 10^{-6} \text{ V }^\circ C^{-2}$.
questions.solution:
The thermo-emf $E$ developed in a thermocouple when the cold junction is at $0^\circ \text{C}$ and the hot junction is at $T^\circ \text{C}$ is given by the relation:

$E = aT + \dfrac{1}{2}bT^2$

Given:
$a = -46 \times 10^{-6} \text{ V }^\circ \text{C}^{-1}$
$b = -0.48 \times 10^{-6} \text{ V }^\circ \text{C}^{-2}$
$T = 0.001^\circ \text{C} = 10^{-3} ^\circ \text{C}$

Substituting the values into the formula:

$E = (-46 \times 10^{-6})(10^{-3}) + \dfrac{1}{2}(-0.48 \times 10^{-6})(10^{-3})^2$

$E = -46 \times 10^{-9} - 0.24 \times 10^{-12}$

Since the second term is negligibly small compared to the first term, it can be ignored:

$E \approx -46 \times 10^{-9} \text{ V}$

$E = -4.6 \times 10^{-8} \text{ V}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: Determine the thermo-emf developed in a copper-silver thermocouple if the junctions are maintained at $0^\circ C$ and $40^\circ C$. Use the data from the table.
questions.solution:
From standard thermoelectric data, the Seebeck coefficients for copper and silver are $S_{Cu} = 2.76 \mu\text{V}/^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $S_{Ag} = 2.50 \mu\text{V}/^{\circ}\text{C}$.

The relative Seebeck coefficient for a copper-silver thermocouple is:

$S_{Cu-Ag} = S_{Cu} - S_{Ag} = 2.76 - 2.50 = 0.26 \mu\text{V}/^{\circ}\text{C}$

The thermo-emf $E$ developed for a temperature difference $\Delta T$ is:

$E = S_{Cu-Ag} \times \Delta T$

Given the junctions are at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $40^{\circ}\text{C}$, $\Delta T = 40^{\circ}\text{C}$.

$E = 0.26 \times 10^{-6} \times 40 = 10.4 \times 10^{-6} \text{ V} = 1.04 \times 10^{-5} \text{ V}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: Determine the neutral temperature and the inversion temperature of a copper–iron thermocouple when the reference junction is maintained at $0^\circ C$. Use the data provided in the table.
questions.solution:
For a copper-iron thermocouple, the neutral temperature $T_n$ is a known standard value, which is $270^{\circ}C$.

The relationship between the inversion temperature $T_i$, neutral temperature $T_n$, and the temperature of the cold junction $T_c$ is given by $T_i - T_n = T_n - T_c$.

Given that the reference junction is maintained at $T_c = 0^{\circ}C$, the equation simplifies to $T_i = 2T_n$.

Substituting the value of $T_n$, we get $T_i = 2 \times 270^{\circ}C = 540^{\circ}C$.

Thus, the neutral temperature is $270^{\circ}C$ and the inversion temperature is $540^{\circ}C$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: Determine the charge required to pass through an electrolyte in order to liberate one atom of a monovalent material.
questions.solution:
For a monovalent material, the valency is $1$, which means one electron is involved in the liberation of one atom at the electrode.

The charge required to liberate one atom is equal to the magnitude of the charge of one electron.

$q = e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$

Alternatively, using Faraday's laws of electrolysis, the charge required to liberate one mole ($N_A$ atoms) of a monovalent substance is $1 \text{ F} \approx 96500 \text{ C}$.

The charge required for one atom is:

$q = \dfrac{F}{N_A} = \dfrac{96500}{6.022 \times 10^{23}} \approx 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: Determine the charge required to pass through an electrolyte in order to liberate one atom of a divalent material.
questions.solution:
A divalent material requires $2$ electrons to reduce one ion into a neutral atom.

The charge of one electron is $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.

The total charge required to liberate one atom is $q = 2e$.

Substituting the value of $e$, we get $q = 2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C} = 3.2 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: Determine the amount of silver liberated at the cathode if a current of $0.500 \text{ A}$ flows through an $\text{AgNO}_3$ electrolyte for $1$ hour. The atomic weight of silver is $107.9 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
Using Faraday's first law of electrolysis, the mass of the substance deposited at the electrode is given by:

$m = ZIt$

where $Z$ is the electrochemical equivalent, $I$ is the current, and $t$ is the time.

$Z = \dfrac{M}{nF}$

For the deposition of silver from $\text{AgNO}_3$, the reaction is $\text{Ag}^+ + e^- \rightarrow \text{Ag}$. Thus, $n = 1$.

Given:
$M = 107.9 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$
$I = 0.500 \text{ A}$
$t = 1 \text{ hour} = 3600 \text{ s}$
$F = 96500 \text{ C mol}^{-1}$

Substituting the values:

$m = \dfrac{107.9 \times 0.500 \times 3600}{1 \times 96500}$

$m = \dfrac{107.9 \times 1800}{96500}$

$m = \dfrac{1942.2}{96500} \approx 2.01 \text{ g}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: An electroplating unit deposits $3.0 \text{ g}$ of silver onto a brass plate over a period of $3.0$ minutes. Determine the current utilised by the unit. The electrochemical equivalent of silver is $1.12 \times 10^{-6} \text{ kg C}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
According to Faraday's first law of electrolysis, the mass deposited is given by $m = ZIt$, where $Z$ is the electrochemical equivalent, $I$ is the current, and $t$ is the time.

Given:
$m = 3.0 \text{ g} = 3.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg}$
$t = 3.0 \text{ minutes} = 3.0 \times 60 \text{ s} = 180 \text{ s}$
$Z = 1.12 \times 10^{-6} \text{ kg C}^{-1}$

Substituting the values into the formula:
$I = \dfrac{m}{Zt}$

$I = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{-3}}{1.12 \times 10^{-6} \times 180}$

$I = \dfrac{3000}{201.6} \approx 14.9 \text{ A}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: Determine the time needed to liberate $1.0$ litre of hydrogen at STP in an electrolytic cell using a current of $5.0 \text{ A}$.
questions.solution:
The reaction for the liberation of hydrogen gas at the cathode is:

$2H^{+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow H_2$

From the stoichiometry, $2 \text{ moles}$ of electrons ($2 \text{ F}$ of charge) are required to produce $1 \text{ mole}$ of $H_2$ gas.

At STP, $1 \text{ mole}$ of an ideal gas occupies $22.4 \text{ L}$.

Number of moles of $H_2$ in $1.0 \text{ L}$ is $\dfrac{1.0}{22.4} \text{ mol}$.

Charge required, $Q = 2 \times \dfrac{1.0}{22.4} \times 96500 \text{ C} = \dfrac{96500}{11.2} \text{ C}$.

Using the formula $Q = I \times t$, where $I = 5.0 \text{ A}$:

$t = \dfrac{Q}{I} = \dfrac{96500}{11.2 \times 5.0} \text{ s} = \dfrac{19300}{11.2} \text{ s} \approx 1723.2 \text{ s}$

Converting time into minutes:

$t = \dfrac{1723.2}{60} \text{ minutes} \approx 28.72 \text{ minutes}$

This is approximately $29 \text{ minutes}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: Two voltameters, one containing a solution of silver salt and the other a solution of a trivalent-metal salt, are connected in series. A current of $2 \text{ A}$ is maintained for $1.50$ hours. It is observed that $1.00 \text{ g}$ of the trivalent metal is deposited. Determine the atomic weight of the trivalent metal.
questions.solution:
According to Faraday's first law of electrolysis, the mass of the substance deposited is given by:

$m = \dfrac{M}{nF} I t$

where $M$ is the atomic weight, $n$ is the valency, $F$ is Faraday's constant ($96500 \text{ C mol}^{-1}$), $I$ is the current, and $t$ is the time in seconds.

Given:
$m = 1.00 \text{ g}$
$n = 3$ (for a trivalent metal)
$I = 2 \text{ A}$
$t = 1.50 \text{ hours} = 1.50 \times 3600 \text{ s} = 5400 \text{ s}$

Substituting the values into the formula:

$1.00 = \dfrac{M \times 2 \times 5400}{3 \times 96500}$

$M = \dfrac{1.00 \times 3 \times 96500}{2 \times 5400}$

$M = \dfrac{289500}{10800}$

$M = 26.8 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: Two voltameters, one containing a solution of silver salt and the other a solution of a trivalent-metal salt, are connected in series. A current of $2 \text{ A}$ is maintained for $1.50$ hours. It is observed that $1.00 \text{ g}$ of the trivalent metal is deposited. Determine the amount of silver deposited during this period, given that the atomic weight of silver is $107.9 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
According to Faraday's first law of electrolysis, the mass of a substance deposited at an electrode is given by:

$m = \dfrac{E I t}{F}$

For silver, the valency is $1$, so its equivalent weight $E_{\text{Ag}}$ is equal to its atomic weight:

$E_{\text{Ag}} = 107.9 \text{ g eq}^{-1}$

The total charge passed through the series circuit is:

$Q = I \times t = 2 \text{ A} \times (1.50 \times 3600) \text{ s} = 10800 \text{ C}$

Substituting the values into the formula:

$m_{\text{Ag}} = \dfrac{107.9 \times 10800}{96500}$

$m_{\text{Ag}} = \dfrac{1165320}{96500} \approx 12.075 \text{ g}$

Rounding off to one decimal place, the mass of silver deposited is $12.1 \text{ g}$. The data regarding the trivalent metal is extraneous.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: A brass plate with a surface area of $200 \text{ cm}^2$ on one side is electroplated with $0.10 \text{ mm}$ thick silver layers on both sides using a $15 \text{ A}$ current. Determine the time taken to complete the job. The specific gravity of silver is $10.5$ and its atomic weight is $107.9 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
Total surface area to be electroplated (both sides) $= 2 \times 200 = 400 \text{ cm}^2$

Thickness of the silver layer $= 0.10 \text{ mm} = 0.01 \text{ cm}$

Volume of silver deposited $= \text{Area} \times \text{Thickness} = 400 \times 0.01 = 4 \text{ cm}^3$

Mass of silver deposited, $m = \text{Volume} \times \text{Density} = 4 \times 10.5 = 42 \text{ g}$

According to Faraday's first law of electrolysis:

$m = \dfrac{M}{nF} I t$

For silver, the valency $n = 1$. Substituting the given values:

$42 = \dfrac{107.9}{1 \times 96500} \times 15 \times t$

$t = \dfrac{42 \times 96500}{107.9 \times 15} \text{ s}$

Converting the time into minutes:

$t = \dfrac{42 \times 96500}{107.9 \times 15 \times 60} \text{ min}$

$t = \dfrac{4053000}{97110} \text{ min} \approx 41.73 \text{ min}$

Rounding off to the nearest integer, the time taken is approximately $42 \text{ minutes}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: As shown in the figure, a current is passed through an electrolyte of $\text{AgCl}$. It is observed that $2.68 \text{ g}$ of silver is deposited on the cathode in $10$ minutes. Determine the heat developed in the $20 \Omega$ resistor during this period. The atomic weight of silver is $107.9 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
According to Faraday's first law of electrolysis, the mass of the substance deposited is given by:

$m = ZIt = \dfrac{M}{nF}It$

Substituting the given values ($m = 2.68 \text{ g}$, $M = 107.9 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$, $n = 1$, $F = 96500 \text{ C mol}^{-1}$, $t = 600 \text{ s}$):

$2.68 = \dfrac{107.9}{1 \times 96500} \times I \times 600$

$I = \dfrac{2.68 \times 96500}{107.9 \times 600} \approx 4 \text{ A}$

The heat developed in the resistor is given by Joule's law of heating:

$H = I^2Rt$

Using $R = 20 \Omega$ and $t = 600 \text{ s}$:

$H = (4)^2 \times 20 \times 600$

$H = 16 \times 12000 = 192000 \text{ J}$

$H = 1.92 \times 10^5 \text{ J} \approx 1.9 \times 10^5 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: When connected to a silver voltameter, the potential difference across the terminals of a battery having an emf of $12 \text{ V}$ and an internal resistance of $2 \Omega$ drops to $10 \text{ V}$. Determine the amount of silver deposited at the cathode in half an hour. The atomic weight of silver is $107.9 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The terminal potential difference of the battery is given by $V = E - Ir$.

Substituting the given values, $10 = 12 - I(2)$.

$2I = 2 \Rightarrow I = 1 \text{ A}$.

The time for which the current flows is $t = 30 \text{ min} = 1800 \text{ s}$.

The total charge passed through the voltameter is $Q = It = 1 \times 1800 = 1800 \text{ C}$.

According to Faraday's first law of electrolysis, the mass of silver deposited is $m = ZQ$, where $Z$ is the electrochemical equivalent.

$Z = \dfrac{\text{Atomic weight}}{\text{Valency} \times F} = \dfrac{107.9}{1 \times 96500} \text{ g C}^{-1}$.

$m = \dfrac{107.9}{96500} \times 1800 = \dfrac{107.9 \times 18}{965} \approx 2.01 \text{ g}$.

The amount of silver deposited is approximately $2 \text{ g}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: A plate having an area of $10 \text{ cm}^2$ is to be electroplated with copper (density $9000 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$) to a thickness of $10$ micrometres on both sides, utilising a $12 \text{ V}$ cell. Determine the energy expended by the cell during the deposition process. If this energy is subsequently used to heat $100 \text{ g}$ of water, determine the rise in the water's temperature. Given the ECE of copper is $3 \times 10^{-7} \text{ kg C}^{-1}$ and the specific heat capacity of water is $4200 \text{ J kg}^{-1} \text{ K}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
Volume of copper deposited on both sides of the plate:

$V = 2 \times A \times t$

$V = 2 \times (10 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^2) \times (10 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}) = 2 \times 10^{-8} \text{ m}^3$

Mass of copper deposited:

$m = \rho V = 9000 \times 2 \times 10^{-8} = 1.8 \times 10^{-4} \text{ kg}$

From Faraday's law of electrolysis:

$m = ZQ \Rightarrow Q = \dfrac{m}{Z}$

$Q = \dfrac{1.8 \times 10^{-4}}{3 \times 10^{-7}} = 600 \text{ C}$

Energy expended by the cell:

$E = Q \times V_{\text{cell}} = 600 \times 12 = 7200 \text{ J} = 7.2 \text{ kJ}$

Rise in temperature of water:

$E = m_w s \Delta T$

$7200 = 0.1 \times 4200 \times \Delta T$

$\Delta T = \dfrac{7200}{420} = \dfrac{120}{7} \approx 17.14 \text{ K}$

Thus, the energy expended is $7.2 \text{ kJ}$ and the rise in temperature is approximately $17 \text{ K}$.
